Ekemini Simon, a senior reporter at PREMIUM TIMES, has won the 2026 Ray Ekpu Prize for Investigative Journalism in Akwa Ibom State.
This is the fifth time he has won the first prize in the competition set up in 2021 by Inoyo Toro Foundation in honour of Ray Ekpu, the co-founder of Newswatch magazine and the 1987 International Editor of the Year.
Mr Simon emerged as the overall winner at the Inoyo Toro Foundation’s 2026 ceremonies for the 19th Teacher’s Award and sixth Ray Ekpu Awards for Investigative Journalism, held on Friday in Uyo, Akwa Ibom State.
He won the award for a two-part investigation exposing oil companies’ continued gas flaring in violation of Nigerian laws and the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission’s ( NUPRC ) failure to enforce the country’s anti-gas-flaring regulations.
The investigation, titled Oil companies violate Nigerian laws, flare gas, face no sanctions and NUPRC fails to enforce Nigeria’s anti-flaring law as methane emissions go unchecked , examined regulatory failures and the continued environmental consequences of gas flaring in the Niger Delta.
Mr Simon previously won the prize four times while working with TheMail newspaper before securing his latest recognition with PREMIUM TIMES.
He has featured in all six editions of the competition and was runner-up in 2024, when Assistant Editor at PREMIUM TIMES, Cletus Ukpong, emerged winner.

Joseph Atainyang of The Watchman Post came second in the 2026 edition with his four-part investigation, Stalling a Dream: Inside Struggles of University of Maritime Studies, Oron .
Announcing the results, the Chairman of the Screening Committee, Nsikak Essien, a former editor of the defunct National Concord newspaper and former Chairman of the Board of Pioneer Newspapers, said the 2026 competition received only five entries, down from 22 in 2025.
Mr Essien, however, said the quality of the entries had generally improved compared with the previous edition, when, according to him, one-third of the submissions did not qualify as investigative reports.
He expressed concern that no woman journalist submitted an entry this year, compared with two female participants in the 2025 edition.
“In intellectual engagement, women are always top. Why is it different for investigative journalism? I encourage women to take part in investigative journalism and apply,” he said.
Mr Essien said the committee had maintained a minimum score of 70 per cent for the first three positions, but only two entries met the benchmark this year, leaving the third position vacant.
He said the decision was meant to preserve the award’s credibility and standard rather than distribute prizes to entries that did not meet the required threshold.
Other members of the screening committee were Ini Uko, a professor of English and Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic) of the University of Uyo; Nsibiet John, Chairman of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), Akwa Ibom State Council; Akpandem James, a former managing editor of Daily Independent; Kayode Komolafe, Deputy Managing Director of ThisDay and a board member of the Inoyo Toro Foundation; and Umoh Joshua, Secretary of the Committee.
The overall winner received N1 million, while the first runner-up received ₦500,000. Although the 2026 edition increased the total prize money to ₦1.75 million, the ₦250,000 earmarked for the second runner-up was not awarded.
The award was initially introduced with a ₦500,000 prize for the overall winner. Its prize structure expanded in 2024 to accommodate two additional positions after Thompson and Grace Investment Limited joined as sponsors.
The 2026 edition recorded a further increase in the prize purse, with the Ibom Heritage Cultural Organisation and Umoh Joshua joining the Inoyo Toro Foundation as sponsors.
In his remarks, Mr Simon thanked the Inoyo Toro Foundation and other sponsors for sustaining the award, saying their investment would encourage investigative journalism and motivate more journalists to pursue accountability reporting.
He described himself as the competition’s biggest beneficiary, having won it five times and also finished as runner-up in 2024.
He pledged to support other journalists interested in investigative journalism, particularly those willing to commit the time and resources required to produce impactful reports.
“The field is ripe, but the harvesters are few. We call on journalists to rethink their work and prioritise investigative journalism, because that is what really impacts society.
“Nothing gladdens the heart of a journalist as the result or impact he gets from his work. When we put in our best, we contribute significantly to making our society better. But when journalists go to sleep, the decay becomes aggravated, and the journalist who is part of the society is also affected,” he said.
The NUJ Chairman in Akwa Ibom, Mr John, said investigative journalism often demands considerable sacrifices from practitioners, sometimes at the expense of their personal and family comfort.
He said journalists who undertake such work deserve recognition and commended the Inoyo Toro Foundation for sustaining the award.
The sixth edition marked the first time veteran journalist Ray Ekpu attended the ceremony of the journalism prize named in his honour.
Mr Ekpu thanked Mr Inoyo and his family for establishing the award, describing the gesture as recognition of excellence beyond ethnic or local government affiliations.
He said he neither came from Mr Inoyo’s local government area nor shared his tribal background, adding that the foundation’s decision to honour him reflected an appreciation of professional excellence.
“Udom Inoyo is a man who understands the meaning of excellence. He sees a man and says this is excellence and celebrates him,” he said.
Mr Ekpu said he had nominated Mr Essien to serve on the screening committee because of his experience working with him and his reputation for being tough, diligent and professional.
Addressing the award winners and other journalists, he described journalism as a profession built on truth-telling and charged practitioners to remain prepared to face the consequences of speaking truth to power.
He encouraged the winners not to rest on their achievements but to continue working towards greater recognition, including international awards.
Mr Ekpu identified extensive reading and a strong sense of justice as essential qualities of a successful investigative journalist.
“The secret to being an outstanding investigative journalist is that you have to read well,” he said, disclosing that his personal collection contained up to 10,000 books.
He cautioned journalists against relying solely on online encyclopaedias such as Wikipedia, which he said could contain errors, and urged them to cultivate the habit of reading books.
He also advised journalists to let injustice disturb them, arguing that such sensitivity could drive them toward credible investigations with meaningful social impact.
Mr Ekpu further asked journalists to remain humble, dress appropriately, and avoid letting professional achievements make them arrogant.
Recounting his experience under military rule, he said he was detained six times for his courageous journalism but never abandoned the profession. “I was still publishing. Remain courageous,” he told the journalists.
The Ray Ekpu Prize was established by Mr Inoyo to promote journalistic excellence, strengthen accountability in public office, combat corruption and impunity, defend human rights, and encourage national unity and ethnic cohesion.
The competition is open to registered NUJ members of Akwa Ibom origin, including journalists practising outside the state.
PREMIUM TIMES had earlier reported the expansion of the prize money to ₦1.75 million for the 2026 edition and the history of the initiative.
The newspaper also previously reported the recognition of its journalists in the competition. In 2024, Assistant Editor at PREMIUM TIMES Cletus Ukpong won the top prize for an investigation exposing the wrongful dismissal of a University of Uyo lecturer, while Saviour Imukudo emerged first runner-up in 2025.
